summary:
NISAR Earth Pulse is an interactive web map that turns radar data from the new NASA–ISRO NISAR satellite into surface-change maps that anyone can read. Floods, fires and other disasters often hit when clouds, smoke or darkness block optical satellites, so responders lose sight of the ground just when they need it most. NISAR’s L-band radar sees through cloud and rain, works day and night, and revisits every location every 12 days. Its data is free, but reading it usually takes specialist SAR software and training.

We built a Python pipeline that downloads NISAR Level-2 GCOV products from NASA’s ASF DAAC, calibrates and filters them, and detects change between passes. It then measures the changed area in km² and publishes the results to a lightweight browser app. Users can swipe between before and after images, switch between HH, HV and RGB radar views, and play a 12-day timeline with a chart of flooded area. Plain-language notes explain what the radar signal means. Disaster teams, farmers, insurers, city planners and students can all use NISAR’s view of a changing Earth without being radar experts.
details:
What it does
NISAR Earth Pulse is an interactive web map that shows how Earth’s surface changes over time, using radar data from the NASA–ISRO NISAR satellite. A user picks a study area and an event, such as a monsoon flood, and compares NISAR passes taken 12 days apart. The app shows what changed, how much area was affected in km², and why the radar signal looks the way it does.

How it works

  1. Data: We download NISAR L-band Level-2 GCOV (geocoded backscatter) products from NASA’s ASF DAAC.
  2. Processing: A Python pipeline converts the backscatter to decibels, applies a speckle filter and clips the data to the study area.
  3. Change detection: We compare before and after passes using the dB difference and a water threshold. Calm floodwater reflects the radar pulse away from the satellite, so flooded land turns dark in HH. Flooded trees and buildings cause double-bounce scattering, so they look brighter.
  4. Measurement: For each pass, we calculate the changed or flooded area in km² to build a time series.
  5. Web app: The results are exported as map layers and shown on a lightweight static HTML/JavaScript site that needs no server.

Features

  • A before/after swipe slider to compare any two dates
  • HH, HV and RGB polarization views to tell apart water, vegetation and urban areas
  • A 12-day timeline with playback and a chart of flooded area over time
  • Optional context layers: Sentinel-2 optical imagery, ESA WorldCover land cover and population density
  • A plain-language “What is happening here?” panel that explains the radar signal and likely causes
  • GeoTIFF download and shareable views

Benefits and impact
Optical satellites are blind under cloud, smoke and darkness, which is exactly when floods, fires and storms are at their worst. NISAR’s L-band radar works day and night, through cloud and rain, and partly through vegetation. Its data is free, but using it normally takes SAR expertise. Our app removes that barrier so these groups can use it:

  • Disaster response teams can see flooded areas on every pass, even under cloud.
  • Farmers and insurers can check crop-field flooding.
  • City planners can spot areas that flood every monsoon.
  • Students and the public can learn how radar sees Earth by exploring real NASA data.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages: Python for data processing; HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the web app
  • Environment: Google Colab
  • Python libraries: [e.g., NumPy, rasterio/GDAL, h5py, matplotlib]
  • Mapping: [e.g., Leaflet / MapLibre]
  • Data: NISAR GCOV (ASF DAAC), Sentinel-2, ESA WorldCover, [population dataset, e.g., WorldPop]
  • Hosting: [e.g., GitHub Pages]
  • Hardware: no special hardware; it runs entirely in the cloud and the browser

What makes it creative
Most SAR tools are built for specialists and show raw images. We turned radar physics into a visual story: you can swipe through time, switch polarizations to see different surface types, and read a plain-language explanation next to the map. Combining radar with optical, land-cover and population layers shows both what changed and who was affected.

What our team considered

  • Accessibility: a clear interface, simple language and a static site that loads quickly on low bandwidth
  • Scientific accuracy: we used analysis-ready GCOV products and checked water detection against Sentinel-2 on clear days
  • Scalability: the pipeline works for any study area and can rerun on each new NISAR pass
  • Limitations: speckle noise, wind-roughened water, and steep terrain that can create radar shadow
  • Future work: automatic updates on every new pass, InSAR ground motion for subsidence and landslides, and flood alerts for nearby communities
